parts.title: How a Ketogenic Diet and Intermittent Fasting Change Body Chemistry and a Brain Hormone Called Orexin-A: A 12-Month Randomized Trial in Adults with Obesity
parts.abstract:
Background/Objectives: More and more researchers are studying two ways of eating, intermittent fasting and the ketogenic diet, to see whether they help the body's chemistry in people with obesity. Intermittent fasting means going without food for set stretches of time. The ketogenic diet is very low in carbohydrates and high in fat. However, we still know little about how these diets affect the brain and hormones over a long time. This is especially true for Orexin-A, a small protein-like molecule made in the brain that is thought to help control how the body uses energy. Our aim was to compare how different diets affect body chemistry, inflammation and Orexin-A over a long period in adults with obesity.

Methods: In this 12-month trial, 30 adults with obesity (a body mass index, or BMI, of 30 kg/m2 or more) were randomly assigned to one of three groups, in equal numbers. The first group followed a low-calorie ketogenic diet (KD). The second followed a 16:8 time-restricted eating plan (TRF16:8), which means eating only within an 8-hour window each day. The third followed a 5:2 intermittent fasting plan (ADF5:2), which means eating normally on five days and eating very little on two days. At the start and every 3 months, we measured body size and body fat, blood sugar after fasting, blood fats, inflammation markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF-α and IL-10) and Orexin-A in the blood. We checked that people stuck to their diets through structured food logs and monthly check-ups. We analysed the data with statistical models that take into account that each person was measured several times. We also ran extra checks that took age and sex into account.

Results: Everyone finished the trial. Over 12 months, the ketogenic diet gave the biggest lasting drops in BMI, body fat, fasting blood sugar and total cholesterol. The 16:8 plan brought faster improvements in body chemistry early on, and it showed the most steady rise in Orexin-A over time. The 5:2 plan gave moderate improvements across the measures. In every group, people whose Orexin-A went up also showed signs of better metabolic flexibility (the ability to switch between burning sugar and burning fat) and less inflammation. However, our analyses of whether Orexin-A might be a link between diet and these changes were only exploratory and cannot show cause and effect. The differences between groups stayed statistically significant for body fat, blood sugar and the pattern of change in Orexin-A, even after we adjusted for the fact that we made many comparisons.

Conclusions: The ketogenic diet was linked to the strongest long-term improvements in body chemistry. The 16:8 plan gave faster early results and the most stable rise in Orexin-A. These findings show that different diets lead to different changes in body chemistry and in the brain's control of energy. Because our group was small, the results should be read with caution. Larger trials are needed to make clear whether Orexin-A could serve as a measurable sign of how the body responds to diet in obesity.
parts.introduction_first: Obesity is one of the biggest health problems facing the world in the 21st century. It is closely linked to metabolic syndrome (a cluster of problems such as high blood sugar and high blood pressure), insulin resistance (when the body stops responding properly to insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar), type 2 diabetes, heart and blood vessel disease, and a long-lasting, low-level inflammation [1]. As obesity has become more common, many researchers have looked for diets that work well, can be kept up for a long time, and help the body use energy more efficiently while reducing the illnesses that come with obesity. Two promising approaches have stood out [2]. The first is the ketogenic diet (KD), a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet that makes the body produce ketone bodies, which are fuel molecules made from fat. The second is time-restricted feeding, also called intermittent fasting, where people eat only within a set window of time each day. In people with obesity, ketogenic diets have been shown to reduce the fat stored around the organs inside the belly, improve blood sugar and blood fat levels, and raise the levels of Orexin-A, a small protein-like molecule made in the hypothalamus, a part of the brain that helps control hunger and energy use (also known as hypocretin-1) [3].
parts.conclusion:
5. Conclusions

Our study shows that both the ketogenic diet and 16:8 intermittent fasting bring large improvements in body fat, in measures of body chemistry, and in inflammation in people with obesity. These benefits were strongly linked to rises in Orexin-A in the blood, which points to a possible role for Orexin-A in helping the brain and body adjust to a new way of eating. Our findings suggest that Orexin-A moves in the opposite direction to BMI, body fat, fasting blood sugar and total cholesterol: when Orexin-A goes up, these tend to go down. This supports the idea that Orexin-A helps the body switch between burning sugar and burning fat. The ketogenic diet and 16:8 fasting are also effective diets that people can keep up for a long time, and both can boost the activity of the orexin system. The 5:2 plan had weaker effects on body chemistry and on the brain's control of energy. This suggests that how consistently a diet is followed, and how much it engages the body's energy pathways, are key to how the body adapts. Orexin-A stands out as a promising measurable sign for checking how diets affect the brain's control of energy, and it may be a useful tool in personalized nutrition for managing obesity. In short, the ketogenic diet gave the largest and longest-lasting improvements in body chemistry, while the 16:8 plan gave quick early benefits and a steady response in the brain's energy signals. These findings are early results and should be read with caution because our group was small. Larger randomized trials are needed to confirm what we saw.

Our study has several limitations. First, we closely checked whether people followed their diets through structured food logs and regular interviews about what they had eaten. However, we did not use blood or urine tests to confirm that the ketogenic diet group actually reached ketosis, the state in which the body is burning ketone bodies for fuel (for example, by measuring β-hydroxybutyrate in the blood or ketones in the urine). Because of this, we cannot directly measure how much ketosis each person reached or how steady it was. Instead, we relied mainly on what people told us about their diets, and people may not always report their eating accurately.

Second, our group was fairly small and covered a narrow range of ages. This may mean our findings do not apply as well to other groups of people with different backgrounds or health conditions. Random assignment made sure the groups were similar at the start, but we cannot fully rule out some differences between individual people.

Third, we measured many things: body size, body chemistry, inflammation and brain hormones. When many tests are run, there is a greater chance of a false alarm, called a type I error, where a difference appears to be real when it is not. We adjusted the follow-up comparisons within each measure, and we treated our main measures as more important than our secondary and exploratory ones. Even so, findings from the secondary and exploratory measures should be read with caution.

Fourth, we studied Orexin-A as an exploratory sign, and the amount of Orexin-A in the blood may not fully show how active the orexin system is in the brain. So any conclusions about how the brain controls energy should be seen as early ideas that are meant to spark further research, not as proven explanations.

Finally, we ran extra checks that took age and sex into account, and these confirmed that our main findings held up. However, because we only observed links between Orexin-A and other measures, and because our analyses of whether Orexin-A might be a link between diet and these changes were exploratory, we cannot say for certain that one causes the other. Future studies with larger groups, and with direct measurements of the brain's energy signals, are needed to better understand how diet affects the body's use of energy.
parts.introduction_rest:
The orexin system is made up of two small protein-like molecules, Orexin-A and Orexin-B, and the two receptors they attach to, called OX1R and OX2R. Receptors are like locks on cells that a molecule fits into, so that the cell can respond. The orexin system is best known for helping us stay awake, alert and hungry. However, more and more evidence shows that it also plays a bigger part in how the body keeps its energy in balance, in how much we move around on our own, and in how the body adjusts its use of energy. For example, people with obesity had statistically significantly lower levels of Orexin-A in their blood than people with a normal weight [4,5,6,7]. (A difference is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone.) This suggests that Orexin-A is involved in how the human body uses energy and stores fat.

In experiments with animals, stronger orexin signals have been linked to more movement on their own and to animals being less likely to become obese from a high-fat diet. Orexin-A has also been linked to the control of the heart and blood vessels, to switching on the sympathetic nervous system (the part of the nervous system that prepares the body for action, such as by raising heart rate), and to the development of high blood pressure in people with obesity. Together, these findings show that orexin helps connect the brain with the body's use of energy [8,9].

At the same time, ketogenic diets and intermittent fasting have been shown to change not only body size, body fat and body chemistry, but also the signals that pass between the brain and the body's hormones. When the body is in ketosis, it makes more ketone bodies, mainly two called acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate. Studies have shown that these ketone bodies can act as an extra fuel for the cells lining the colon, the last part of the gut. They also help keep the gut lining healthy, calm inflammation and reduce the growth of cancer in the gut. Being in ketosis may also affect the body's daily rhythms, such as the sleep-wake cycle, and the way the hypothalamus controls energy balance [10,11,12].

Even with all this, we still do not know well how diet, inflammation, body fat and orexin signals work together in people with obesity [13,14,15].

To help fill this gap, we set out to study how three different diets affect body fat, body chemistry and Orexin-A in the blood over 12 months in people with obesity. The three diets were the ketogenic diet, the 16:8 time-restricted eating plan and the 5:2 plan. We expected that diets which do a better job of improving metabolic flexibility (the ability to switch between burning sugar and burning fat) and of reducing the fat stored around the organs inside the belly would also lead to bigger rises in Orexin-A in the blood. In this way, the rise in Orexin-A would reflect the brain and body adjusting to the new diet. Our findings may give new insights into how the brain and hormones help explain the way diet affects obesity. They may also support using Orexin-A as a measurable sign when planning diets.

Intermittent fasting has been studied a great deal for its effects on weight loss, metabolic flexibility and blood sugar control. Recent research also suggests that the changes in body chemistry that come with fasting may interact with orexin signals, which are often lower in people with obesity. However, no one has yet compared different kinds of fasting over a long time, with people randomly assigned to each kind, while also tracking Orexin-A as a possible link between diet and the changes in the body. As far as we know, no earlier study has directly compared a low-calorie ketogenic diet, a 16:8 eating plan and a 5:2 plan over 12 months while following how Orexin-A changes over time. Our trial therefore fills an important gap. It is the first long-term study with three groups, randomly assigned, that looks at how these diets affect body chemistry and the brain's control of energy. It also explores whether changes in Orexin-A may partly explain the changes in body chemistry in adults with obesity.
parts.methods:
2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Who Took Part

We recruited 30 adults with obesity, 15 men and 15 women, aged 20 to 40 years. They came from the Dietetics, Sports Medicine, and Psychophysical Well-being Unit of the University Hospital "Luigi Vanvitelli" (University of Campania), which is run by Professor Marcellino Monda. During their first medical check-up, we explained three ways of eating that are commonly used in everyday care for people with obesity. The first was a low-calorie ketogenic diet (KD). The second was a 16:8 time-restricted eating plan (TRF16:8). The third was a 5:2 intermittent fasting plan (ADF5:2).

We then followed the participants for 12 months, with regular checks of their body chemistry and hormones. We did not assign anyone to a diet, and we did not change their usual care. To take part, people had to be aged 20 to 40 and have obesity, meaning a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m2 or more, as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO). We measured body fat, but we did not use it to decide who could join. People also had to have kept their weight steady (within 3 kg either way) over the previous 3 months, and not have been in any organized diet program during the previous 6 months.

We left people out if they had type 1 or type 2 diabetes, heart and blood vessel disease, hormone disorders, were pregnant or breastfeeding, smoked, had a long-lasting inflammatory condition, had a psychiatric illness, took weight-loss medicines, or took any medicine known to affect how the body handles sugar or fats. These rules helped make sure the people in our study were alike in their body chemistry. We checked what medicines people were taking at every visit. No one started or stopped a medicine that could affect body chemistry during the study. Everyone gave written permission to take part before joining. We followed the Declaration of Helsinki, a set of ethical rules for research with people, and the Ethics Committee of the University of Campania "Luigi Vanvitelli" approved the study (protocol 0003232/1, 1 February 2023).

2.2. How the Study Was Set Up

This was a 12-month study in which we observed three ways of eating that are commonly used in everyday advice for people with obesity: a low-calorie ketogenic diet (KD), a 16:8 time-restricted eating plan (TRF16:8), and a 5:2 intermittent fasting plan (ADF5:2). We did not try to change anything. We simply compared the groups as they were.

Once the groups were chosen, we followed each person from the start (which we call T0) to 12 months later (T3), checking their body chemistry and hormones again and again. We did not use random assignment, any method of placing people into groups, or any way of hiding who was in which group. This is because we were not testing a treatment. Instead, we wanted to see the natural differences between people who follow diets that are already part of everyday medical care.

Our research team did not change anyone's usual care, did not give any advice beyond standard diet advice, and did not introduce any experimental treatment. Everything we did followed a design in which we only observed and measured, without trying to change anything. Our focus was on following the same people over time and recording what happened.

2.3. The Diets

We set up three diets to compare how they affect the body's use of energy, inflammation, and the prevention of the problems with body chemistry that come with obesity.

The ketogenic diet (KD) gave people about 1200 calories a day, with very few carbohydrates (50 g or less per day). Most of the diet was fat (70–75% of calories), with a moderate amount of protein (20–25%). We chose this mix of nutrients to bring people into ketosis, the state in which the body is burning ketone bodies for fuel, and to keep them there for the whole study. The KD group followed the same low-calorie plan, so that everyone would reach ketosis. We know that the number of calories each person needs is different. However, this fixed limit matches the ketogenic plans doctors use to manage obesity.

We checked whether people followed the diet every day in the early afternoon (between 2:00 and 4:00 p.m.). To do this, we measured ketones in a drop of blood taken from a finger, using GD40 Delta test strips (TaiDoc Technology Co., New Taipei City, Taiwan). We counted a person as being in ketosis when their level of β-hydroxybutyrate, one of the ketone bodies, was above 0.5 mmol/L.

The 16:8 plan meant that people went without food for 16 hours in a row each day and ate only within an 8-hour window, for example from 12:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. They ate about the same total number of calories a day as the ketogenic diet group, but spread over that shorter window. During the eating hours, 40–45% of calories came from carbohydrates, 30–35% from fats (mainly healthy mono- and polyunsaturated fats), and 20–25% from protein. During the fasting hours, people could drink water, black coffee and unsweetened tea. This pattern of long fasting periods followed by controlled eating makes the body more flexible in how it uses energy. It helps people get better at burning fat and makes the body respond better to insulin.

The 5:2 plan meant that people had two fasting days each week, not in a row (for example, Monday and Thursday). On those days, they ate only 20–25% of the energy they normally need, about 500–600 calories a day. On the other five days, 30% of calories came from carbohydrates, 45% from fats (mainly omega-3 and other unsaturated fats), and 25% from protein. People chose lean protein, vegetables, fruits that do not raise blood sugar quickly, and small amounts of healthy fats. On the remaining five days, they ate as much as they wanted. This plan copies the effect of cutting calories now and then while still letting people eat freely most of the week. This kind of structure is known to help people stick to a diet and to improve their body chemistry.

2.4. How We Tracked and Measured Things

We took measurements at the start (T0) and again at regular times (T1, T2 and T3) over 12 months.

We collected the following measurements:

2.4.1. Body Size and Body Fat

-

We measured weight and height with standard instruments.

-

We calculated BMI as weight divided by height squared (kg/m2).

-

We measured body fat using bioimpedance analysis (BIA). This method sends a tiny, harmless electrical current through the body and uses how the body resists it to estimate how much fat, muscle and water are inside. We used a machine that uses several frequencies (BIA 101 Anniversary, Akern Srl, Florence, Italy). We always measured under the same conditions: people had fasted for at least 8 hours, had an empty bladder, and had not done intense exercise in the previous 24 hours. BIA estimates body fat, lean muscle, total body water, and the water inside and outside the cells, which gives a detailed picture of what the body is made of.

We checked whether people followed their diets through weekly food logs and through structured interviews about what they had eaten at each visit. We also used changes in body fat (from BIA) and in body chemistry as indirect signs of whether people were sticking to their diets.

2.4.2. Blood Chemistry

-

We took blood from a vein in the morning, after people had fasted for at least 8 hours. The blood went into tubes containing EDTA, a substance that stops blood from clotting. We spun the tubes in a centrifuge at 3000 rpm for 15 minutes at 4 °C to separate the plasma, the liquid part of the blood. We divided the plasma into small portions and stored them at −80 °C until we tested them.

-

We measured blood fats (total cholesterol, HDL, LDL and triglycerides) and blood sugar. We measured Orexin-A in the serum (the liquid part of the blood) using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). This is a lab test that uses antibodies to detect a particular substance. We used ready-made kits made for each of these markers (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).

2.5. How We Analysed the Data

We did all our statistics with two computer programs, IBM SPSS Statistics (version 28.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and R (version 4.3.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). We made the graphs with GraphPad Prism (version 10.1; GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA).

For measurements that can take any value, such as weight or blood sugar, we report the average (mean) together with the standard deviation (SD), which shows how spread out the values are around the average. We used the Shapiro–Wilk test to check whether the values followed the usual bell-shaped pattern, and Levene's test to check whether the values were spread out by similar amounts in each group. Some tests also assume that the spread of values is similar across groups, a condition called sphericity. When this was not true, we used the Greenhouse–Geisser correction, which adjusts the test so that it does not give false alarms. For every test, we called a result statistically significant when p < 0.05 (two-tailed). This means that if there were really no difference, a gap as large as the one we saw would turn up by chance alone less than 5% of the time.

First, we checked whether the groups were similar at the start. For measurements that can take any value, we used a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), a test that compares the averages of several groups. When the data did not follow the usual pattern, we used the Kruskal–Wallis test instead, which does a similar job without that assumption. For things that fall into categories, such as yes or no, we used the χ2 (chi-square) test or Fisher's exact test. Table 1 shows the starting values and how the groups compared.

To study body size, blood chemistry and hormones, we used a two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA). This test looks at two things at once. The first is time (T0, T1, T2 and T3), which is the same for everyone. The second is the diet (ketogenic diet, 16:8 fasting or 5:2 fasting), which differs between people. The test also checks for an interaction between time and diet, which asks whether the change over time was different in different diet groups.

When we found a significant effect of time, of diet, or of the interaction, we followed up with Tukey's honestly significant difference (HSD) tests. These compare pairs of groups or time points while adjusting for the fact that we made many comparisons. We used them for two purposes: (i) to compare each group with itself at each time point against the start (T0), and (ii) to compare the groups with each other at each time point (T0, T1, T2 and T3).

For each RM-ANOVA, we report the F value (a number that shows how big the differences are compared with the natural spread of the data), the degrees of freedom (df, numbers linked to how much data went into the test), the p value, and the partial eta-squared (η2). The eta-squared shows how much of the variation in the data is explained by each factor, so it tells us how big an effect is. We judged the size of the effects using Cohen's rules: small at 0.01 or more, medium at 0.06 or more, and large at 0.14 or more.

Because we ran many repeated-measures tests on many different measures, we recognize that the chance of false alarms (type I errors) could grow when we look across all the results. To reduce this risk and make the results easier to understand, we gave priority to the main measures that matter most in medicine: BMI, body fat, fasting blood sugar, total cholesterol and Orexin-A. We treated the other blood chemistry and inflammation markers as secondary and exploratory, and we interpreted them cautiously, only when they made biological sense and agreed across our analyses. Within each measure, we used the Tukey-adjusted follow-up comparisons to control for the many comparisons we made.

To explore how changes in body chemistry were linked to changes in the brain's control of energy, we calculated Pearson's correlation coefficients (r). A correlation coefficient is a number between −1 and 1 that shows how closely two things rise and fall together. We compared the change in Orexin-A (the value at T3 minus the value at T0) with the changes in BMI, body fat, blood sugar and total cholesterol. When the values did not follow the usual bell-shaped pattern, we used Spearman's rank correlations (ρ), which work on the order of the values rather than their exact size.

We also wanted to know whether changes in Orexin-A might be the link between the diet and the changes in body chemistry. To test this, we used hierarchical linear regression and mediation analyses, run with the PROCESS macro (Model 4) for SPSS. In these analyses, the diet group was the starting factor, the change in Orexin-A was the possible link (the mediator), and the change in BMI or the change in blood sugar was the outcome. We tested the indirect effect, meaning the part of the diet's effect that might pass through Orexin-A, using bootstrapping. In bootstrapping, the computer draws many new samples from our own data (here, 5000) to see how much the result could vary. This gave us 95% confidence intervals (CIs) that were corrected for bias. A confidence interval is a range of values that shows how precise an estimate is. We judged how well each model fitted the data using the coefficient of determination (R2), which shows how much of the variation the model explains. We also checked that the factors in each model were not too closely tied to each other, using variance inflation factors (VIF < 2), so that we could leave out such problems. We tested all results in a two-sided way, which means we looked for differences in either direction. We showed the results as averages with standard deviations, or as scatter plots with lines showing how Orexin-A was linked to the body chemistry measures.

To check that our main findings held up, and to get estimates adjusted for other factors, we ran extra checks that took age and sex into account. For this, we used linear mixed-effects models. These are statistical models that take into account that each person was measured several times. For each measure, the models included the diet group, time, and the interaction between group and time as fixed effects, meaning the main factors we wanted to study. Age and sex were added as covariates, meaning extra factors that the model takes into account. Each person also had their own starting level (a random intercept), which allows for the fact that a person's repeated measurements are linked to each other. From these models, we worked out adjusted averages (estimated marginal means) and the differences between groups over time, each with a 95% confidence interval.
parts.results:
3. Results

At the start of the study, the three diet groups were alike in their background, body size, body chemistry and brain hormones (Table 1). We found no statistically significant differences between the groups in BMI, body fat, fasting blood sugar, total cholesterol or Orexin-A in the blood. In other words, the groups were similar in how much obesity they had, in their body chemistry and in their brain hormone levels when the study began. This confirms that the groups were well matched before anyone started their diet (Table 1).

BMI was similar in all three groups at the start (Table 1). Over time, though, BMI changed by different amounts in each group. Statisticians call this a "time × group interaction": the way a measure changes over time depends on which group a person is in (Table 2). From the start (T0) to the end of the study (T3), the ketogenic diet (KD) gave the biggest drop in BMI, from 33.4 ± 2.9 to 29.1 ± 2.5 kg/m2, a change of −4.3. The 16:8 plan came next, with BMI falling from 33.7 ± 3.0 to 30.4 ± 2.6 kg/m2 (a change of −3.3). The 5:2 plan changed the least, from 34.3 ± 3.2 to 33.5 ± 3.0 kg/m2 (a change of −0.8). The number after each ± shows how much the values varied around the average.

At the end of the study, BMI was significantly lower in the KD group than in the 5:2 group (p = 0.004; Table 2). We used a Tukey adjustment, which makes the test stricter because we compared several pairs of groups. The difference between the KD and 16:8 groups was not significant (p = 0.11). Overall, both the KD and the 16:8 plan lowered BMI over 12 months, and the KD lowered it the most (Figure 1).

Body fat was also similar in all groups at the start (Table 1). It changed by different amounts in each group over time (time × group interaction; Table 2). From T0 to T3, the KD group lost the most body fat, from 34.7 ± 3.1% to 28.9 ± 2.7% of body weight (a change of −5.8). The 16:8 group lost less, from 36.2 ± 3.3% to 31.6 ± 2.9% (a change of −4.6). The 5:2 group changed the least, from 38.1 ± 3.5% to 35.8 ± 3.1% (a change of −2.3). At the end of the study, body fat was significantly lower in the KD group than in the 5:2 group (Tukey-adjusted p = 0.006; Table 2). The difference between the KD and 16:8 groups was not significant (p = 0.14). Overall, the KD and the 16:8 plan both reduced body fat over 12 months, and the KD reduced it the most (Figure 2).

Total cholesterol was similar in all groups at the start (Table 1). It changed by different amounts in each group over time (time × group interaction; Table 2). From T0 to T3, the KD group had the biggest drop, from 252 ± 23 to 196 ± 18 mg/dL (a change of −56). The 16:8 group dropped from 250 ± 24 to 205 ± 19 mg/dL (a change of −45), and the 5:2 group from 251 ± 25 to 230 ± 22 mg/dL (a change of −21). At the end of the study, total cholesterol was significantly lower in the KD group than in the 5:2 group (Tukey-adjusted p = 0.008; Table 2). The difference between the KD and 16:8 groups was not significant (p = 0.16). Overall, these findings show that the KD lowered blood fats more strongly over 12 months (Figure 3).

Fasting blood sugar was similar in all groups at the start (Table 1). It changed by different amounts in each group over time (time × group interaction; Table 2). From T0 to T3, the KD group had the biggest drop, from 108 ± 8 to 87 ± 6 mg/dL (a change of −21). The 16:8 group dropped from 110 ± 9 to 95 ± 7 mg/dL (a change of −15), and the 5:2 group from 112 ± 9 to 106 ± 8 mg/dL (a change of −6). At the end of the study, fasting blood sugar was significantly lower in the KD group than in the 5:2 group (Tukey-adjusted p = 0.007; Table 2). The difference between the KD and 16:8 groups was not significant (Table 2). Overall, these findings show that the KD lowered blood sugar more strongly over 12 months (Figure 4).

Orexin-A in the blood was similar in all groups at the start (Table 1). It changed by different amounts in each group over time (time × group interaction; Table 2). From T0 to T3, the KD group had the biggest rise, from 2.1 ± 0.3 to 3.4 ± 0.4 ng/mL (a change of +1.3). The 16:8 group rose from 2.0 ± 0.3 to 3.0 ± 0.4 ng/mL (a change of +1.0), and the 5:2 group from 2.1 ± 0.3 to 2.6 ± 0.3 ng/mL (a change of +0.5). At the end of the study, Orexin-A was significantly higher in the KD group than in the 5:2 group (Tukey-adjusted p = 0.006; Table 2). The difference between the KD and 16:8 groups was not significant (p = 0.12). Overall, these findings show a stronger response in the orexin system with the KD over 12 months (Figure 5).

Table 1 also sums up the Tukey-adjusted comparisons between pairs of diet groups at each time point. At the start (T0) and in the early months (T1 and T2), we found no significant differences between any groups for any of the measures. At the end of the study (T3), however, the KD group showed significantly bigger changes than the 5:2 group for BMI, body fat, fasting blood sugar, total cholesterol and Orexin-A. For the body size and body fat measures, we found no significant differences between the KD and 16:8 groups.

To look at all the measures together, we used a statistical method called a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA. It tests how much time, diet and the two together affect each measure, while taking into account that each person was measured several times. We used it for body size, body chemistry and hormones. As Table 3 shows, every measure had a significant overall effect of time (p < 0.001), meaning people improved steadily over the 12 months. Every measure also had a significant time × group interaction (p ≤ 0.01). This shows that the size of the change, and the way it unfolded over time, differed from one diet to another.

For every measure, the KD brought the strongest and most consistent changes, followed by the 16:8 plan. The 5:2 plan gave smaller or slower effects. The effects were generally large. We measured the size of an effect with a number called η2, which shows how much of the variation in a measure is linked to the factors we studied. Here it ranged from 0.41 to 0.50. The statistical models also explained 45–52% of all the variation in each measure (R2 = 0.45–0.52), which supports how solid these findings are.

In extra checks that took age and sex into account, we used linear mixed-effects models, a type of statistical model that allows for repeated measurements of the same people. These checks confirmed our main findings, and the time × group interaction stayed statistically significant for the main measures. People on the KD had the biggest drops in BMI, body fat, blood sugar and total cholesterol, and a clear rise in Orexin-A. The 16:8 plan gave similar but slightly smaller improvements. The 5:2 plan led to only small changes, especially in body fat and in how well blood sugar and blood fats were controlled. These results show that both the KD and the 16:8 plan worked well in changing body chemistry and the brain's control of energy, and that the KD was the strongest and longest-lasting of the three (Table 3).

Table 4 sums up the results at the end of the study. All three diets were linked to improvements in body size, body chemistry and brain hormones over the 12 months, but the size of these improvements clearly differed between diets. The KD brought the biggest changes. Compared with the start, it gave the largest drops in BMI (−4.3 kg/m2 at T3), body fat (−5.8%), fasting blood sugar (−21 mg/dL) and total cholesterol (−56 mg/dL), and the biggest rise in Orexin-A in the blood (+1.3 ng/mL). The 16:8 plan also brought meaningful improvements, though smaller than the KD. The 5:2 plan was linked to smaller changes, or to changes that were not significant. Overall, these end-of-study results confirm a ranking of how well the diets worked, with the KD bringing the strongest and most consistent changes in body chemistry and in the brain's control of energy.

To look more closely at how the brain and body chemistry might be connected, we compared the change in Orexin-A (from T0 to T3) with the changes in the main measures of body chemistry. We used correlation, which shows how closely two measures rise and fall together. The correlation is given as a number, r, that runs from −1 to +1. A minus sign means that when one goes up, the other tends to go down. A plus sign means they tend to move in the same direction.

We found a strong link in the opposite direction between the change in Orexin-A and the change in BMI (r = −0.62, p < 0.001) and in body fat (r = −0.58, p < 0.001). In other words, people whose Orexin-A rose more tended to lose more body fat. In the same way, the change in Orexin-A was negatively linked with the change in blood sugar (r = −0.54, p = 0.002) and in total cholesterol (r = −0.49, p = 0.005). This suggests that people with a stronger rise in Orexin-A generally had better metabolic flexibility and better control of blood sugar. We also found a positive link between the change in Orexin-A and the change in lean mass, the weight of muscle and other tissue that is not fat (r = +0.46, p = 0.007). This further supports a helpful connection between the brain's control of energy and keeping the body's active tissue.

When we looked at each diet group separately, the KD and 16:8 groups showed the strongest links (r values between 0.55 and 0.70, ignoring the minus sign; p < 0.01). The 5:2 groups showed weaker links, or links that were not significant (p > 0.05).

Next, we wanted to know whether Orexin-A might be a link between diet and the changes in body chemistry. For this, we used hierarchical linear regression, a method that adds factors to a model step by step to see how much each one matters. In these models, the diet was the starting factor, the change in Orexin-A was the possible link, and the change in BMI or blood sugar was the outcome. In the full model, the diet significantly predicted the change in BMI (β = −0.53, p < 0.001) and in blood sugar (β = −0.48, p = 0.002). The β value shows how strongly the diet predicts the outcome, and a minus sign means a bigger drop.

When we added the change in Orexin-A to the model, the diet's predictive effect became smaller (β = −0.32, p = 0.01 for BMI; β = −0.28, p = 0.03 for blood sugar). At the same time, the change in Orexin-A stayed a significant predictor on its own (β = −0.38, p = 0.004 for BMI; β = −0.35, p = 0.006 for blood sugar). The part of the diet's effect that passed through Orexin-A was statistically significant. Its 95% confidence interval, the range in which the true value most likely lies, ran from −0.29 to −0.08. This part made up about 35% of the total variation in the drop in BMI and 30% of the improvement in blood sugar. This confirms that Orexin-A partly links diet to the benefits for body chemistry. Taken together, these results suggest that a rise in Orexin-A plays a central role in helping the body switch between burning sugar and burning fat, in helping it use fat for fuel, and in keeping blood sugar and blood fats balanced.

These findings support the idea that changes in the brain's control of energy, through Orexin-A, may be a key biological pathway linking time-restricted feeding and the way the body runs on fat to better body chemistry in obesity (Figure 6).

4. Discussion: What Our Results Mean

In this study, we looked at the long-term effects of three ways of eating on body chemistry and on the brain's control of energy in adults with obesity. The three were the ketogenic diet (KD), the 16:8 time-restricted eating plan, and the 5:2 fasting plan. Overall, both the ketogenic diet and the 16:8 plan led to statistically significant improvements in body size and body fat and in measures of body chemistry. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. Alongside these improvements, Orexin-A in the blood rose clearly. The 5:2 plan, by contrast, caused only small changes in most measures, and these were not statistically significant. These results show that different diets affect the body's chemistry in quite different ways. They also point to Orexin-A as a possible measurable sign that helps the brain and body adjust to a diet kept up over a long time.

One of the most important things we saw was the large improvement in body size and body fat with the ketogenic diet and the 16:8 plan. BMI and body fat fell significantly, while lean body mass (the weight of muscle and other tissue that is not fat) went up. This matches earlier research showing that time-restricted eating and the ketogenic diet reduce fat and improve how the body uses energy, by helping it burn more fat and by lowering insulin levels [16,17,18].

We also checked how closely the changes in Orexin-A moved together with the changes in other measures. To do this, we used a number called a correlation, written r. It runs from −1 to 1. A value near 1 means two things tend to rise together, a value near −1 means one tends to fall as the other rises, and a value near 0 means there is little link. The more Orexin-A changed, the more BMI and body fat changed in the opposite direction: r was −0.62 for BMI and −0.58 for body fat. This suggests that people whose orexin system became more active also saw bigger improvements in their overall body make-up. This fits with evidence that people with obesity tend to have lower Orexin-A levels. It also supports the idea that bringing orexin activity back up may help people lose weight and release fat from their stores [19,20,21,22].

Turning to body chemistry, the ketogenic diet and 16:8 groups had significant drops in fasting blood sugar and total cholesterol. This fits with better control of blood sugar and better use of fats as fuel. These changes were strongly linked to rises in Orexin-A: the more Orexin-A went up, the more blood sugar and total cholesterol went down (r = −0.54 for blood sugar and r = −0.49 for total cholesterol). Orexin-A is known to switch on the sympathetic nervous system, the part of the nervous system that gets the body ready for action. It also makes people move around more on their own and burn more heat without exercising. Together, these effects help the body switch between burning sugar and burning fat and help it use different fuels [23,24,25]. The links we found support the idea that Orexin-A may act as a messenger that brings different signals together, helping the body move into a more efficient way of using energy when people change what they eat.

We also ran analyses of whether Orexin-A might be a link between diet and these changes. These showed that changes in Orexin-A partly explained the effects of the diets on BMI and blood sugar. The part of the effect that passed through Orexin-A explained about 35% of the drop in BMI and about 30% of the improvement in fasting blood sugar. This suggests that Orexin-A is not just a sign that the body is improving. It may also play an active part in the benefits we saw.

The ketogenic state, in which the body makes more ketone bodies (one of them is called β-hydroxybutyrate), may also boost orexin signals. It may do this by adjusting the energy sensors in the hypothalamus and by keeping nerve cells firing steadily. This could make the body use energy more efficiently and reduce inflammation. This fits with reports that ketone bodies help calm inflammation and serve as fuel for tissues that use a lot of energy [13,26,27].

When we compared the three diets, clear differences stood out. The ketogenic diet gave the biggest improvements in every measure. The 16:8 plan was also helpful, but its effects were slightly smaller. The 5:2 plan had weaker effects on body chemistry and did very little to activate the orexin system. These differences suggest that how steady and regular the timing of eating is may play a key role in how the brain and body adjust [28]. Time-restricted eating creates regular fasting periods, which may help the orexin nerve cells in the brain line up better with the body's daily clock. The ketogenic diet, meanwhile, keeps up signals driven by ketone bodies, which may work together with the orexin system. The small effects of the 5:2 plan suggest that cutting calories now and then, without regular fasting or ketosis, may not be enough to strongly switch on the orexin system [29].

Taken together, these findings highlight Orexin-A as a central controller that links eating patterns, the body's ability to switch between fuels, and inflammation. Orexin-A was strongly linked to improvements in body fat, blood sugar, blood fats and lean mass. This points to a bigger picture in which orexin signals are a key part of how the body reshapes the way it uses energy.

Orexin-A is widely known as a key controller of how much energy the body uses and of how it gets into an active state. Besides its main job of keeping people awake, Orexin-A switches on the sympathetic nervous system, helps the body burn fat, boosts the heat made by brown fat (a type of fat that burns fuel to produce heat), and makes people move around more on their own. Together, these effects help people burn more energy each day [30,31,32,33,34]. Experiments have shown that orexin signals make mitochondria, the tiny power stations inside cells, work harder. They also help the body switch between fuels and make it easier to move between burning sugar and burning fat [35,36,37,38].

Obesity usually goes along with lower orexin activity. This is partly because long-lasting inflammation holds back the orexin nerve cells, through chemical messengers called cytokines that send signals to slow them down [39,40,41]. So the steady rise in Orexin-A we saw during the trial may reflect not only the brain and hormones adjusting directly to the diets, but also the body being freed from the slowing effect of inflammation. This return of orexin activity fits with the better ability to switch between fuels, the greater use of fat, and the higher energy use. These processes may partly explain the good results in body chemistry that we saw in the diet groups, especially in diets that help the body's daily clock stay steady and reduce inflammation [31,42]. Our analyses suggested that Orexin-A may partly explain some of the changes in body chemistry, but they cannot show cause and effect. Only experiments that directly change the orexin system, or medicines that act on it, could prove for certain that one causes the other.

This supports the idea that boosting the orexin system, either through ways of eating or possibly through medicines, could be a promising direction for managing obesity [43,44].

Our study has some limitations. Our group was fairly small (30 people), although this is similar to other studies of diet. We checked whether people followed their diets, but they may still have reported their eating inaccurately. The ketogenic group followed a low-calorie ketogenic diet, so we may not be able to compare it directly with ketogenic diets that provide the same number of calories. Finally, we had no group that did not follow any of the diets, so we cannot separate out the full effect of each diet on its own.

Our study provides evidence that both the ketogenic diet and the 16:8 plan bring large benefits in body chemistry and in the brain's control of energy in people with obesity, and that these benefits largely pass through rises in Orexin-A. These findings show that Orexin-A could be a useful measurable sign for checking how diets work in medical care. They also support the role of carefully chosen diets in improving how the body uses energy.

Even so, our study has several limitations. The group was small, the study took place at a single centre, and neither the participants nor the researchers knew which group each person was in. The diets also cut calories by different amounts, and we relied on what people told us about following their diets. We did not measure sleep and physical activity in detail, and our analyses of whether Orexin-A might be a link between diet and these changes were exploratory. The strengths of our study include its 12-month length, the random assignment of people to three groups, and the way we looked at body chemistry, inflammation and brain hormones together.
